An event names its kind, author and URL, never the text: comments come from anyone who can comment, and the agent reads them through the URL as data. `.claude/skills/watch-pr/SKILL.md` says when to run it. Comments by the pull request's author and by the `gh` user are not events.  Ready needs every check that the base branch's rules require, by name, present and green on two equal polls, an approval, no unresolved thread, no draft, and a mergeable state. On a base without rules, such as a stacked pull request's, every check counts as required. Every failed check is an event. Cancellations are separate events.  Exit codes: 0 ready or merged; 1 only action can make it ready (a failed required check, a conflict, changes requested, an unresolved thread or a draft on a green head, closed, or GitHub refused); 2 bad arguments, an unknown pull request, or no repository.  Adapted from `pr-wait` in tstack (https://github.com/t3dotgg/tstack, MIT, © 2026 Theo Browne).

reason: constraint: Routes a scheduled image rescan to a tracking issue instead of a red status.  A drift finding is not a regression anyone can revert: no commit introduced it, and the repository is exactly as correct as it was yesterday. A second blocking gate on that is how a team learns to ignore the gate, so this reads the `.policy.json` files `scan-main-images.ts` and `scan-upstream-images.ts` wrote and keeps one issue in step with them — created when findings appear, edited in place when the finding set changes, silent when it has not, and closed when it clears. Kyverno's `sync-trivy-issues` has the same shape.  Supported-release failures use the same planner with a separate marker. They can happen before reports exist, so they update the run link without interpreting partial policy results; maintainers close that issue after triage and a successful rescan.  The issue is identified by an HTML marker carrying a fingerprint of the finding set, not by its title: a title is editable, and a run that cannot recognise its own issue opens a duplicate every week until someone turns the schedule off.

reason: constraint: The commit whose published images a run aliases for every component its diff left alone.  A run based on the default branch aliases from its own base, whose images that branch's own run published. A layer of a stacked pull request is based on another branch's head, which published nothing and belongs to no merged pull request, so the chain of bases is walked until a commit the default branch contains. A run that reaches none has nothing to alias and builds every image itself.  A pull request aliases only from a default-branch commit whose own run has published its images. Right after a merge, the default branch's newest commit is still being built, so the run builds every image itself instead of aliasing images that do not exist yet.

reason: constraint: A runtime retains this lease until it releases its prepared inputs. Erasure cannot acknowledge deletion while another process can still write or read the attempt. context: <module> -> public final class BoundedTranscript {
reason:
constraint: A container's output, collected whole unless it is enormous, and never silently cut.

A review's transcript is the only account of what it did: which practices it observed, what it was refused and why, where its time went. Keeping a prefix loses the ending, where a run says how it failed; keeping a suffix loses the beginning, where it says what it was asked and what it read. So everything is kept until a run is large enough to threaten the collecting process, and past that point both ends are kept with a line between them saying exactly how much is missing — a reader is never left to wonder whether they are looking at the whole thing. None of it is written to the application's own log.

reason:
constraint: DB-backed JWK source for Hephaestus-issued JWTs. Acts as a Spring Security {@link JWKSource} (consumed by {@code NimbusJwtEncoder} and {@code NimbusJwtDecoder}).

Bootstrapping

On first run (empty {@code jwt_signing_key} table), {@link #ensureActiveKey()} generates a P-256 EC key pair. The private PKCS#8 DER bytes are sealed at rest by {@link JwtSigningKeySealer} (AES-256-GCM under the system master key) and stored tagged {@code encryption_key_id = JwtSigningKeySealer.KEY_ID}. The database migration seals legacy private keys before runtime starts. Startup and key materialization refuse unsealed rows.

Key lifecycle

A single active key signs all tokens; re-keying today means deploying with a fresh key (the old row is left {@code active=true} and still verifies until manually retired). Zero-downtime, NATS-coordinated rotation across pods is not yet implemented — see ADR 0017 for the planned design.

Hot-path

{@link #get(JWKSelector, SecurityContext)} is called on every JWT encode/decode. We resolve from an {@link AtomicReference}-cached {@link JWKSet}, refreshed from DB on TTL expiry ({@value #CACHE_TTL_MILLIS} ms).

context: <module> -> public class ClusterLock {
reason:
constraint: Serializes work by name across every server process, for work that calls a provider or the broker and so must not hold a transaction (docs/contributor/transactions.md). An in-memory lock serializes only one process.

The lock is a PostgreSQL session lock on a connection of its own, without a transaction. PostgreSQL drops it with the connection, so a process that dies leaves no lock behind. A waiting caller polls rather than blocks in {@code pg_advisory_lock}: a statement that waits there holds a transaction open, and a migration's {@code CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY} waits for every open transaction. Each attempt borrows a pooled connection and returns it at once when the lock is taken elsewhere, so waiters cannot hold the connections that the holder's work needs. Names hash to 32 bits, so two names can share a lock: that costs only a wait, never a missed one.

Not re-entrant: each call takes its own connection, so work that calls again for the same name waits for itself until its wait ends.

context: <module> -> "System-wide rate-limit tracking — records Outline API limits per server origin across all workspaces")
reason:
constraint: Per-scope Outline API rate-limit tracker. Purely observational: Outline throttling is enforced by the {@code Retry-After}-honoring 429 handling in {@link OutlineApiClient}, so this class never blocks or paces — it only records what Outline actually told us, and feeds the {@link RateLimitSnapshot} SPI the Outline admin page renders.

Outline reports a budget ONLY on a 429

Outline's rate-limiter middleware sets {@code Retry-After}, {@code RateLimit-Limit}, {@code RateLimit-Remaining} and {@code RateLimit-Reset} exclusively inside its 429 catch block ({@code server/middlewares/rateLimiter.ts}); successful responses carry none of them. Two consequences shape this class:

  • A healthy Outline connection can never show a live gauge. "Not reported" is the normal steady state, not a degraded one — and when the operator sets {@code RATE_LIMITER_ENABLED=false} it is the permanent one. This tracker therefore records throttle events, not a budget.
  • What a 429 reports ({@code remaining ≈ 0}) is true only for the instant it was reported. The shared window-expiry rule in {@link RateLimitSnapshot#observed} retires it once the window lapses, so an observed exhaustion cannot freeze on the admin page as if it were current.

{@code Retry-After} — not {@code RateLimit-Reset} — is the reliable reset signal. Outline emits it as {@code msBeforeNext / 1000}, i.e. possibly fractional seconds, and emits {@code RateLimit-Reset} as a JavaScript {@code Date.toString()} (e.g. {@code "Sat Jul 18 2026 10:15:00 GMT+0000 (Coordinated Universal Time)"}), which is neither epoch-seconds nor ISO-8601. We therefore parse {@code Retry-After} as a decimal, round it up, and derive the window end from it; {@code RateLimit-Reset} is ignored.

Scope key

The Outline client is stateless with respect to workspace (its methods take {@code (serverUrl, token)}), so the scope is the normalized server origin ({@code scheme://authority}) derived from the request URI on the way out and from the connection's stored {@code serverUrl} at read time (see {@link #scopeOf(String)}). Two workspaces pointing at the same Outline host therefore share one bucket; that is an accepted approximation for a diagnostic, and matches Outline's own per-host rate window.

Null-until-observed

State is created only once real headers arrive, so {@link #snapshot(String)} returns {@code null} until Outline has actually throttled us since the last restart — and the UI omits the row entirely, which for this vendor is the expected long-run display.

Repository removal and workspace purge therefore reach every role's mirrors.

A kept mirror is still a cache. When the volume nears its size, the mirrors that a capture used longest ago go too, because the kubelet would otherwise evict the whole Pod with its running attempts, and the next Pod would fill the same mirrors again. Its next capture fetches it again, as after a restart.

context: <module> -> public class GitHubDeletionSweepService {
reason:
constraint: Deletion reconciliation for issues and pull requests — the half of "sync" that upserts cannot do.

Every other GitHub sync path is upsert-only, so an issue or pull request removed upstream survives locally forever: it is caught only by a webhook, and this deployment's webhooks are not redeliverable (ADR-0008), so a single missed delivery leaves a phantom row that permanently inflates the per-repository counts the admin UI reports. For pull requests it is worse than unreliable — GitHub has no {@code pull_request.deleted} action at all, so a pull request that disappears (repository transfer, staff removal) has no event to miss and no code path to catch it. This sweep is the only mechanism that closes either gap.

The method is a set difference. For each repository it enumerates the complete upstream number set with a number-only GraphQL query ({@code GetRepositoryIssueNumbers} / {@code GetRepositoryPullRequestNumbers}, ~1 rate-limit point per 100 items, versus ~59 for one page of the content query), diffs it against the live local numbers, and tombstones the remainder. It follows the {@code removeStale*} precedent already established for labels, milestones and collaborators rather than inventing a second shape for the same idea.

Fail-closed

A sweep that deletes on bad data is far worse than the phantom row it exists to remove, because the phantom is visible and a wrong deletion is not. So deletion is authorized by provable completeness and nothing else: {@link UpstreamListing#complete()} is true only when pagination ran to {@code hasNextPage == false} with no rate-limit abort, no GraphQL error, no thrown exception, no page-cap truncation, no cancellation, and a node count that agrees exactly with the server's own {@code totalCount}. Any doubt — including any doubt this code did not anticipate, since the flag starts {@code false} and is set only on the one clean exit — skips the repository entirely and deletes nothing. A partial listing is never merged with a previous one.

An empty listing is not evidence of an empty repository

The completeness proof above is a proof about pagination, and pagination is trivially "complete" for a listing that returned nothing: {@code 0 == 0} satisfies the {@code totalCount} cross-check exactly as well as {@code 4000 == 4000} does. That is the one shape where the strongest check in this class has no discriminating power at all, and it authorizes tombstoning the whole repository. Two further guards close it, both fail-closed:
  1. {@code featureDisabled} — a repository whose Issues feature is switched off still answers the {@code issues} connection, with zero nodes and {@code totalCount: 0}. That is indexing state, not deletion: turning Issues back on returns every issue. The sweep selects {@code repository.hasIssuesEnabled} alongside the connection and refuses the listing when it is explicitly {@code false}. Pull requests have no equivalent toggle in GitHub's schema, so only the issue half carries a flag.
  2. {@code emptyUpstreamWithLiveMirror} — independently of any flag, a provably-complete but empty upstream listing is refused whenever the mirror still holds live rows of that class. The two readings of that combination are "every issue in the repository was deleted since the last sync" and "something about this listing is wrong (a narrowed token, an unannounced feature toggle, a vendor bug)". The first is rare and self-heals on the next sync; the second is not, and being wrong costs the whole repository. So the sweep declines and reports degraded rather than deleting on the least trustworthy evidence it can receive.

The cost of both guards is bounded and known: a repository whose issues really were all deleted keeps its phantom rows until a human notices. That is the deliberately cheaper failure.

Tombstone rather than row deletion: see {@code Issue#deletedAt}. Because {@code IssueRepository.upsertCore} clears the tombstone, a repository wrongly swept heals itself on the next ordinary sync — which is the property that makes acting on inference tolerable at all.

context: <module> -> public class GitLabDeletionSweepService {
reason:
constraint: Deletion reconciliation for GitLab issues and merge requests — the half of "sync" that upserts cannot do. The GitLab counterpart of {@code GitHubDeletionSweepService}, reusing the same shared, integration-agnostic tombstone infrastructure ({@code Issue#deletedAt}, {@code IssueRepository#tombstone{Issues,PullRequests}ByRepositoryIdAndNumbers}).

Every GitLab sync path is upsert-only, so an issue or merge request removed upstream survives locally forever. It is worse than for GitHub: GitLab emits no issue- or merge-request-deletion webhook at all, so there is not even a missed event to blame — a deleted issue or MR simply has no code path that would ever notice it, and its phantom row permanently inflates the per-project counts the admin UI reports and keeps feeding practice-review and mentor context as if it were live. This sweep is the only mechanism that closes the gap.

The method is a set difference. For each project it enumerates the complete upstream IID set with a number-only GraphQL query ({@code GetProjectIssueNumbers} / {@code GetProjectMergeRequestNumbers}, a fraction of the complexity of the content queries), diffs it against the live local numbers (GitLab stores each issue/MR under the repository keyed by its per-project {@code iid}, which is the {@code Issue.number} the mirror persists), and tombstones the remainder. It follows the {@code removeStale*} precedent already established for repositories, labels and milestones rather than inventing a second shape for the same idea.

Fail-closed

A sweep that deletes on bad data is far worse than the phantom row it exists to remove, because the phantom is visible and self-correcting and a wrong deletion is not. So deletion is authorized by provable completeness and nothing else: {@link UpstreamListing#complete()} is true only when pagination ran to {@code hasNextPage == false} with no rate-limit abort, no GraphQL error, no circuit-breaker rejection, no thrown exception, no unparseable IID, no page-cap truncation, no cancellation, a {@code count} that was actually observed, and an IID count that agrees exactly with that {@code count}. Any doubt — including a doubt this code did not anticipate, since the flag starts {@code false} and is set only on the one clean exit — skips the entity class entirely and deletes nothing. A partial listing is never merged with a previous one.

An empty listing is not evidence of an empty project

The completeness proof above is a proof about pagination, and pagination is trivially "complete" for a listing that returned nothing: {@code 0 == 0} satisfies the count cross-check exactly as well as {@code 4000 == 4000} does. That is the one shape where the strongest check in this class has no discriminating power at all, and it authorizes tombstoning the entire project. Two further guards close it, both fail-closed:
  1. {@code featureDisabled} — GitLab's {@code IssuesFinder} silently scopes out projects whose Issues feature is switched off ({@code .merge(Project.with_issues_enabled)}), and the merge-request finder behaves the same way. Turning the feature off therefore does not raise an error; it renders as a perfectly well-formed, perfectly "complete" listing of zero items. The sweep now selects {@code project.issuesEnabled} / {@code project.mergeRequestsEnabled} alongside the connection and refuses the listing whenever the relevant flag is explicitly {@code false}. A toggled-off feature hides upstream data; it does not delete it.
  2. {@code emptyUpstreamWithLiveMirror} — independently of any flag, a provably-complete but empty upstream listing is refused whenever the mirror still holds live rows of that class. The two readings of that combination are "every issue in the project was deleted since the last sync" and "something about this listing is wrong (permission scope-out, a feature flag GitLab has not told us about, a vendor bug)". The first is rare and self-heals on the next sync; the second is not, and being wrong costs the whole project. So the sweep declines and reports degraded rather than deleting on the least trustworthy evidence it can receive.

The cost of both guards is bounded and known: a project whose issues really were all deleted keeps its phantom rows until a human notices. That is the cheaper failure.

Tombstone rather than row deletion: see {@code Issue#deletedAt}. context: <module> -> public class SlackRateLimitTracker {
reason:
constraint: Records Slack throttle events per workspace. Unlike its GitHub/GitLab/Outline siblings this tracker is deliberately event-based, not gauge-based.

Why Slack can never report a quota

Slack rate-limits per API method per workspace per app, in tiers whose published numbers are floors rather than budgets ("Tier 2: 20+ per minute", "Tier 3: 50+ per minute"). It sends no remaining/limit headers on successful responses — there is simply nothing to build a {@code remaining / limit} gauge from, and inventing one from the tier tables would violate the honesty rule in {@link RateLimitSnapshot}. This class therefore populates only {@code observedAt} and {@code throttledUntil}, and {@link #snapshot} returns {@code null} until Slack has actually thrown a 429.

What IS observable

A 429 carries {@code Retry-After} in seconds, which yields a real "throttled until T" instant. The state that most needs surfacing is the non-Marketplace clamp on {@code conversations.history} / {@code conversations.replies} (1 request per minute since 2025-05-29), which answers with {@code Retry-After: 60} — an admin currently has no way to see that their Slack sync is crawling for that reason.

Not a pacer

There is no {@code waitIfNeeded} here. Back-off already lives in {@link SlackBackoff#awaitRetry}; this class only watches. Slack's synchronous SDK client never self-throttles (only the async client does), so that hand -rolled catch block is the single point where every 429 is already recognized — and therefore the single point that feeds this tracker.

reason:
constraint: Removes stored messages that Slack no longer holds, as a {@code message_deleted} event would. The event is lost when Slack gives up on delivery or when it ages out of the stream during an outage, and the text would otherwise stay until the retention sweep.

A removal is irreversible, so it needs proof:

  • The stored rows are read before Slack is. A row that exists at that moment was posted before the read, so a message that arrives during the read is never taken for a deleted one. The newest {@link #SETTLING} stay out, so a clock difference or a lagging Slack read cannot make a new message look deleted.
  • A range is compared only after every page of it was read. Any error, an exhausted budget, a consent change or a cancellation removes nothing from it.
  • History holds thread roots only, so a reply is compared only with a complete read of its own thread.
  • Only the last {@link #VISIBLE_HISTORY} are compared, measured when the rows are read: Slack's free plan hides history older than 90 days from the API, so its absence there proves nothing. The day short of 90 absorbs a read that ends later than it starts and a cut that Slack does not specify to the hour.

The pass over older messages never ingests. It reads ranges below the watermark, which can hold paused gaps and messages of people who later opted out, so only a row that is already stored can change.

reason:
constraint: Configuration properties for workspace initialization and management.

This record consolidates all workspace-related configuration under the {@code hephaestus.workspace} prefix. It controls whether a default workspace is automatically initialized at application startup.

Local Development vs Production

This configuration is primarily intended for local development environments where setting up a full GitHub App with webhooks is impractical. In production, workspaces are automatically created via GitHub App installations.

Local Development — GitHub (PAT Mode)

{@code hephaestus: workspace: init-default: true          # Enable GitHub PAT workspace bootstrap default: login: my-github-org      # GitHub org/user to sync token: ghp_xxxxxxxxxxxx   # Personal Access Token repositories-to-monitor: - my-github-org/repo1 - my-github-org/repo2 }

Local Development — GitLab (PAT Mode)

{@code hephaestus: workspace: init-gitlab-default: true       # Enable GitLab PAT workspace bootstrap gitlab-default: login: my-group/subgroup      # GitLab group full path token: glpat-xxxxxxxxxxxx     # Group or Personal Access Token server-url: https://gitlab.example.com  # Optional, for self-hosted }

Production (GitHub App Mode)

{@code hephaestus: workspace: init-default: false         # Disable PAT bootstrap github: app: id: 12345                 # GitHub App ID private-key: ...          # GitHub App private key }

Cross-field validation: When {@code initDefault} is {@code true}, the {@code default.login} and {@code default.token} fields must be provided; otherwise, configuration validation will fail at application startup. @param initDefault whether to initialize a default GitHub PAT workspace at startup (default: {@code false}) @param defaultProperties configuration for the default GitHub workspace; required when {@code initDefault} is {@code true} @param initGitlabDefault Creates a default GitLab workspace with a personal access token at startup. @param gitlabDefault configuration for the default GitLab workspace; required when {@code initGitlabDefault} is {@code true} @param creationPolicy who creates workspaces. Under {@code ADMIN_ONLY}, instance admins create them, and a GitHub App installation waits until an instance admin adopts it. context: <module> -> class WebhookFixtureHandlerResolutionTest extends BaseUnitTest {
reason:
constraint: Mechanical dispatcher round-trip guard. For every committed webhook fixture whose event the system claims to handle, the real routing pipeline (fixture payload → {@code SubjectKeyDeriver} → {@code SubjectParser} → {@link EventTypeKey} → handler-registry lookup) MUST resolve a registered handler. A key that no handler owns is ACK-dropped silently at DEBUG by {@code IntegrationNatsConsumer} — an invisible data-loss bug. This test makes that whole class fail loudly at build time and names the offending fixture.

Unlike per-side unit tests (deriver-only, parser-only), and unlike {@link SubjectGrammarRoundTripTest} (which only proves the publisher subject falls under the consumer's subscription filter), this closes the last link: the parsed {@link EventTypeKey} actually resolves a handler bean. This is the seam that lets an event be handled on one tier yet dead on another — e.g. {@code repository.team} (permission events keyed to a tier with no handler) or GitLab group events.

Ground truth without a Spring context. The set of registered keys is read straight from the production handler classes: every concrete {@link IntegrationMessageHandler} under the kind's package is reflectively constructed with null collaborators (their constructors only assign fields; the {@code EventTypeKey} is built from compile-time literals in the {@code super(...)} call) and its {@link IntegrationMessageHandler#key()} recorded. No database, no beans — but zero drift from reality.

"Claims to handle". A fixture is only required to resolve when its event token is the suffix of some registered key — i.e. the system genuinely handles that event type on some tier. Fixtures for events we deliberately ignore (e.g. {@code deployment}, {@code star}, {@code watch}) have no handler on any tier and are skipped, so this never produces a false failure. The bug it catches is the partial case: an event handled on one tier but silently dropped on another (exactly {@code team}: {@code organization.team} handled, {@code repository.team} was not).

All four integrations are covered. GitHub uses the {@link #resolutionFailures} helper (its {@code X-GitHub-Event} is sourced from the fixture filename, and some filenames encode a payload variant rather than a bare event token, so the claimed-token skip is the right fit there). GitLab, Slack, and Outline read their event token straight from the payload ({@code object_kind}/{@code event_name}, the bolt {@code event.type}, the dotted {@code event} respectively), so they run through the stricter {@link #assertFixturesResolveOrAllowlisted} helper: every committed fixture must EITHER resolve a registered handler OR appear on an explicit, justified allowlist, so a fixture for an event handled on no tier fails the build until someone decides.

constraint: Shutting down a server that runs a scheduled SCM sync.

Each test boots a server context with the production scheduling and lock configuration and the real {@code application.yml}: Boot's task scheduler fires the cron method, the ShedLock advice takes the lock through its own {@link HikariDataSource} and a JPA {@code entityManagerFactory}. Closing that context is the shutdown. The context's DataSource records what the database showed at the moment it was closed. A second {@link JdbcTemplateLockProvider} plays another replica, and the sync-job rows are real. Only provider calls are controlled: the first provider call of a workspace sync waits at a gate. Where a test needs the web drain, Boot's own graceful-shutdown lifecycle runs over a web server whose drain stays open until the test releases it, as an open live-update stream keeps Tomcat's drain open.

context: <module> -> export function reportVisitVitals(router: AnyRouter, queryClient: QueryClient) {
reason: constraint: Measures how a document's page loads and route views felt, and sends each measurement once. The app measures only on an instance whose operator turned page experience metrics on, and only for a document that started on a signed-in page outside a user view: the server counts only signed-in readers, and a refused report would start session recovery. Until both are known, the app does not load `web-vitals`, whose module observes resource timings when it loads.  With `reportSoftNavs`, a browser that detects route changes (Chromium) measures each route view as its own `ROUTE` navigation, and the first view as the `LOAD` navigation. Another browser measures the whole document as one `LOAD`. `web-vitals` reports a navigation's INP and CLS when the next navigation starts, or when the page hides. The first report of each metric is the one sent: a histogram cannot replace a value, so a later report of the same metric is dropped. A page that the back-forward cache restores reports nothing more: `web-vitals` starts late and readies its own restore handling only after timers that a restore can overtake.
